title: Defining and creating structs
summary: Named fields, instances, mutable instances, field init shorthand, struct update syntax, tuple structs, unit-like structs, and who owns a struct's fields.

sections: TRPL 5.1 Using the Field Init Shorthand
TRPL 5.1 Creating Instances with Struct Update Syntax

blocks.md: A tuple groups values by position. A **struct** groups them by **name**. Each piece of data in a struct is a **field**, with a name and a type, so code that uses it reads `user.email` instead of `user.2`. Structs are how you model the things your program is about: a user, a rectangle, a file, a satellite. With enums (next chapter) they are the building blocks of every Rust program's data.

blocks.title: Defining a struct and creating an instance
blocks.explain: The definition is a template; an **instance** fills in concrete values. Fields can be listed in any order when creating an instance. Struct names use **UpperCamelCase**, field names use snake_case.

blocks.title: Changing fields
blocks.md: To change a field, the whole instance must be mutable: `let mut user1 = User { ... };` then `user1.email = String::from("new@example.com");`. Rust does not let you mark only some fields as mutable. Mutability belongs to the variable, not to the type.

blocks.md: To create an instance that is mostly a copy of another, list the fields that differ and finish with `..other`:

blocks.explain: `..user1` takes every remaining field from `user1`. It works like assignment, so it **moves** data: `user1.username` (a String) moves into `user2`, and `user1` can no longer be used as a whole. `active` and `sign_in_count` are `Copy`, and `user1.email` was not used, so those fields of `user1` would still be readable on their own.

blocks.title: Struct update and moves
blocks.md: Run it: the last `println!` fails because `user1.username` moved into `user2`. Fix it by giving `user2` its own `username` (for example `String::from("other")`), so nothing is moved out of `user1` except `Copy` fields. The program should print the two lines in the task.
hints: `User { username: String::from("other"), ..user1 }` copies only `sign_in_count`, which is `Copy`.

blocks.title: Tuple structs
blocks.md: A **tuple struct** has a name but unnamed fields. Use one when naming each field would add nothing, but you want a distinct type. `Color` and `Point` below hold the same three numbers, yet you cannot pass a `Point` where a `Color` is expected. This is the **newtype** idea: wrapping a value in its own type so the compiler keeps different meanings apart.

blocks.explain: Fields are reached by position (`black.0`) or by destructuring. A function `fn climb(by: Meters)` can never be called with feet or seconds by mistake, even though both are plain numbers underneath.

blocks.title: Unit-like structs
blocks.md: A struct can have no fields at all: `struct AlwaysEqual;`. It holds no data, so it takes no memory. That sounds useless, but it becomes handy with traits (chapter 10), where you want a type that has behavior but no state.

blocks.title: Who owns the fields
blocks.md: `User` uses `String` rather than `&str` for its text. That is deliberate: each instance **owns** all its data, and the data lives exactly as long as the instance. A struct can hold references, but then the compiler needs to know the referenced data lives long enough, which requires **lifetimes** (chapter 10). Try it now and you get `error[E0106]: missing lifetime specifier`. Until then, give your structs owned types.

blocks.title: Model a book in a library
blocks.goal: Define a struct, build instances with shorthand and update syntax, and use a newtype.
blocks.behavior:
The starter defines `pub struct Isbn(pub String);` and an empty `pub struct Book`. Complete it and the functions:
- `Book` has public fields `title: String`, `author: String`, `isbn: Isbn`, `year: u16`, `available: bool`.
- `pub fn new_book(title: String, author: String, isbn: Isbn, year: u16) -> Book`: a book that is available. Use field init shorthand.
- `pub fn second_edition(book: &Book, isbn: Isbn, year: u16) -> Book`: a new book with the same title and author (cloned), the new ISBN and year, and available.
- `pub fn describe(book: &Book) -> String`: `"<title> by <author> (<year>)"`, plus `" [on loan]"` when not available.
hints: Fields in a struct are private outside their module unless marked `pub`. The tests are a separate module, so write `pub title: String,` and so on.
`second_edition`: `Book { title: book.title.clone(), author: book.author.clone(), isbn, year, available: true }`.
`describe`: `let mut s = format!("{} by {} ({})", book.title, book.author, book.year);` then push the loan note if needed.
blocks.solution_explain: `second_edition` borrows the original, so it must clone the Strings it reuses; `..*book` would try to move them out of a borrow and fail. `format!` works like `println!` but returns the String instead of printing it.

questions.q: How do you make only the `email` field of a struct instance changeable?
options: You cannot: the whole instance must be `mut`
questions.explanation: Mutability belongs to the binding: `let mut user = ...` makes every field changeable.

questions.q: What does field init shorthand let you write?
questions.explanation: When a variable has the same name as the field, write it once.

questions.q: After `let u2 = User { email: e, ..u1 };` where `User` has a `username: String`, can you still use `u1.username`?
questions.explanation: Struct update syntax moves the non-`Copy` fields it takes.

questions.q: What is a tuple struct good for?
options: Giving a distinct type to a value without naming its fields, like `struct Meters(f64)`
questions.explanation: It is the newtype pattern: same data, different meaning, checked by the compiler.

questions.q: A struct field of type `&str` compiles without any extra annotation.
questions.explanation: Reference fields need a lifetime parameter (chapter 10). Prefer owned `String` for now.

points: `struct Name { field: Type, ... }` defines a type; `Name { field: value, ... }` creates an instance.
Read and write fields with dot notation; the whole instance must be `mut` to change any field.
Field init shorthand: `User { email }` when a variable has the field's name.
Struct update syntax `..other` fills the rest from another instance, moving non-`Copy` fields.
Tuple structs (`struct Meters(f64)`) give a distinct type without field names; unit-like structs have no fields.
Prefer owned field types like `String`; reference fields need lifetimes.

terms.def: A custom type that groups named fields into one value.
A named piece of data inside a struct.
A concrete value of a struct type, with every field filled in.
A struct whose fields have no names, only positions, like struct Color(i32, i32, i32).
A tuple struct wrapping a single value to give it its own type, like struct Meters(f64).
A struct with no fields, useful for implementing traits on a type that holds no data.
